No wording - no question stem, passage, script, answer set or prompt - was copied from IELTS, TOEIC, Cambridge examinations, Aptis, the Duolingo English Test, or any commercial practice material.
contentOriginalityDeclaration.taskStructureNote: Task structures, response formats and prep/response timings follow published task-type conventions that are common across the assessment literature, and are not claimed as novel. In particular the short personal-response speaking task uses a conventional 15s prep / 45s response configuration. Published assessment research informed task structure, construct and rubric dimensions only.

assessment.title: Kiểm tra đầu vào bốn kỹ năng
assessment.description: Bài kiểm tra đầu vào đánh giá Nghe, Đọc, Nói và Viết để xếp lộ trình học phù hợp.
assessment.learnerFacingNote: Kết quả là chỉ dẫn xếp lộ trình học, không phải chứng chỉ trình độ.

clips.internalLabel: Two students deciding to work together
clips.script:
A: Hey, are you heading to the library later?
B: That's the plan. I've still got the slides to finish for our group thing.
A: Same. Should we just do it together? It'd be faster than messaging back and forth.
B: Honestly, yeah. The reading room gets packed after four, though.
A: Then let's aim for three. I'll grab the corner table if I get there first.
B: Deal. I'll bring my laptop and the printouts.

Good morning. A quick note about the study center this week. The second-floor power supply is being rewired, so the computer room up there stays closed until Thursday. The north-side elevators are out of service too, so if you need an elevator, use the south-side ones. The ground-floor group study rooms and the language lab are open as usual, but our online booking system is down, so reserve a room at the desk this week instead. And to print, pick up this week's release code from the front desk; your ID card alone won't start the machines.

clips.internalLabel: Housing office voicemail about a missing signature
clips.script: Hi, this is Mai from the student housing office. I'm calling about the form you dropped off on Monday. Everything you filled in is fine — that's not the problem. It's that we need your current landlord's signature as well, and that page came through blank. If you can get it to us by Friday, we can still process everything this month. Otherwise it rolls into the next cycle, and I'd rather not do that to you.

clips.internalLabel: Presentation that did not go to plan
clips.accentIntent: general American, two distinct voices, conversational
clips.script:
A: So, how was the presentation?
B: Well. Everyone clapped at the end.
A: That's not really an answer.
B: I know. I'd practiced the whole thing twice, and then the projector wouldn't read my file, so I just talked through it from memory.
A: Oh no. For all fifteen minutes?
B: Twelve, in the end. I cut the part I was least sure about.

items.prompt: What are the speakers mainly discussing?
options: Returning some books to the library together
Working on their project together
Finding a quieter place to study
Catching up on a class they both missed
items.answerRationale: Both speakers raise unfinished work on the same group task and agree to do it together; that is the thread of the exchange rather than any single detail.
distractorRationales: A laptop and printouts are mentioned, but no books and no returning.
CORRECT
The reading room filling up after four is mentioned as a reason to go earlier, not as a plan to move elsewhere - the closest competing detail.
A plausible reason two students would meet, but no missed class is mentioned.

items.prompt: What do the speakers agree to do?
options: Meet at three o'clock
Work separately and compare later
Meet after four o'clock
Reserve a room in advance
items.answerRationale: One speaker proposes three and the other accepts with "Deal".
distractorRationales: CORRECT
The opposite of what is agreed; plausible for a listener who catches the messaging remark but not the agreement.
Four is mentioned, but as the time to avoid - a nearby-detail trap.
Nothing is reserved; the corner table remark may suggest booking.

items.prompt: Which area is closed at the start of this week?
options: The language lab
The south-side elevators
The main entrance
The second-floor computer room
items.answerRationale: Stated directly: the computer room upstairs stays closed until Thursday while the second-floor power supply is rewired.
distractorRationales: Named in the same sentence as the group study rooms and described as open as usual.
The north-side elevators are out of service; the announcement sends people to the south-side ones - the strongest mis-attribution.
Not mentioned as closed; a plausible guess for a building with access problems.
CORRECT

items.prompt: How should students reserve a group study room this week?
options: Online
At the desk
By phone
By email
items.answerRationale: Stated directly: the online booking system is down this week, so rooms are reserved at the desk instead.
distractorRationales: The default method a learner would assume, and the one the announcement explicitly rules out this week - this option exists to catch a learner answering from habit rather than from the audio.
CORRECT
A plausible alternative channel the announcement does not offer.
A plausible alternative channel the announcement does not offer.

items.prompt: What do students need in order to print?
options: Their own paper for the printer
Cash for the printing fee
This week's release code
Only their student ID card
items.answerRationale: Stated directly: pick up this week's release code from the front desk. The announcement also rules out the answer a learner would assume from general experience, saying an ID card alone will not start the machines.
distractorRationales: Not mentioned; a plausible requirement in a self-service print room.
No fee is mentioned.
CORRECT
The answer general world knowledge supplies, and the one the announcement explicitly excludes - this option exists to catch a learner who answers without listening.

items.prompt: What does the speaker say about the form?
options: It was submitted after the deadline
Everything on it was filled in incorrectly
It needs to be filled in again from the start
One page came through blank
items.answerRationale: Stated directly: the speaker says the landlord's signature is needed as well and that "that page came through blank".
distractorRationales: The form was dropped off on Monday and the cut-off is Friday, so it is not late - a plausible worry for an administrative call.
Contradicted outright: "Everything you filled in is fine - that's not the problem." The strongest distractor for a learner who hears "problem" and stops.
Only the one blank page is needed, not a fresh form.
CORRECT

items.prompt: Why is the speaker calling?
options: To arrange a meeting about the form
To ask for a payment before Friday
To request one more thing for the form
To explain that the request was refused
items.correctAnswer: To request one more thing for the form
items.answerRationale: The speaker says what was filled in is fine, names one thing still needed, and ties it to a Friday cut-off. The purpose is to obtain that one remaining item in time.
distractorRationales: No meeting is proposed anywhere in the message.
No payment is mentioned; plausible for an administrative call.
CORRECT
Nothing is refused; the speaker is trying to avoid a delay.

items.prompt: What does the speaker suggest about the Friday deadline?
options: Meeting it would avoid a month's delay
It applies only to new applications
It can be extended on request
It was set to suit the student's schedule
items.correctAnswer: Meeting it would avoid a month's delay
items.answerRationale: The speaker contrasts processing this month with rolling into the next cycle and says they would rather not do that - the intention is to convey the consequence, not just the date.
distractorRationales: CORRECT
Plausible if "this month" and "the next cycle" are heard as rules about application types; the message makes no such distinction.
The speaker offers no extension, though the accommodating tone may imply flexibility.
Plausible given the helpful tone, but the date comes from the office's processing cycle, not from the student.

items.prompt: What does the second speaker imply about the presentation?
options: The applause showed that it went well
A technical problem spoiled their plan
The slides were the strongest part
The audience left before it had finished
items.correctAnswer: A technical problem spoiled their plan
items.answerRationale: No negative verdict is stated. The deflection to the applause, the projector failing to read the file, the fallback to speaking from memory and the twelve minutes instead of fifteen must be combined before the implication is available.
distractorRationales: The applause remark read literally - the key literal-interpretation trap.
CORRECT
The speaker never showed slides at all, having spoken from memory - a trap for a learner who missed the equipment failure.
The audience clapped at the end, so they stayed.

items.prompt: What reason does the speaker give for how long the presentation ran?
options: The speaker was asked to stop early
They were given less time than planned
The speaker left out a section
The speaker ran out of time
items.correctAnswer: The speaker left out a section
items.answerRationale: "Twelve, in the end. I cut the part I was least sure about" - the listener must connect the length the speaker reports to the deliberate cut rather than to the equipment problem.
distractorRationales: Nobody intervenes.
A plausible competing cause the conversation never raises.
CORRECT
The speaker attributes the shorter length to cutting a section they were unsure about, not to being stopped by the clock.

passages.text: From March 1, the bicycle racks behind Building C will be removed while the courtyard is repaved. Riders should use the covered racks beside the sports hall instead; these are monitored by camera and hold about ninety bicycles. The arrangement is expected to last eight weeks. During this period, bicycles left against railings or in doorways will be tagged, and if they are not moved within three days they will be taken to the campus store. Anyone collecting a tagged bicycle should bring proof of ownership to the facilities desk, which is open on weekday mornings only.

passages.internalLabel: Why rereading notes feels better than it works
passages.text:
Many students prepare for exams by reading their notes over and over. It feels productive: the material becomes familiar, and familiarity is easily mistaken for knowledge. Researchers who study learning call this the illusion of fluency. Because the words flow smoothly on the fourth reading, the student concludes the content is secure - yet asked to explain it with the page closed, they often cannot.

A more uncomfortable method works better. Putting the notes away and trying to write down what you remember forces the brain to retrieve rather than recognize. Retrieval is slower, and it feels worse, which is exactly why many learners abandon it. Those who persist tend to remember more a week later.

None of this makes rereading useless. It is a reasonable first pass, a way of mapping what is there. The mistake is treating it as the whole of studying rather than the beginning of it.

On the first Saturday of each month, a community hall in the city becomes a repair cafe. People bring broken things - a lamp, a kettle, a jacket with a failed zipper - and sit with a volunteer who helps them fix it. Nobody hands the item over; the owner does the work, guided.

The organizers are deliberate about this. A free repair service would be useful, but it would also leave the owner no better placed the next time something broke. Teaching the repair is slower and messier, and on a busy morning the line grows long. The volunteers accept that trade-off on purpose.

Not everything can be saved. Some appliances are sealed in ways that make opening them impractical, and the cafe keeps a note of which products these are. Over three years that list has grown long enough that the organizers now pass it to a consumer group, which draws on it in its own campaigns.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of the notice?
options: To introduce a charge for bicycle parking
To ask riders to register their bicycles
To report a rise in bicycle theft
To explain where to park bicycles during building work
items.correctAnswer: To explain where to park bicycles during building work
items.answerRationale: Every paragraph serves the temporary relocation and its rules; this is the notice's function.
distractorRationales: No charge appears anywhere.
Proof of ownership is mentioned, which may suggest registration.
Camera monitoring may suggest a theft motive.
CORRECT

items.prompt: What happens to a bicycle left in a doorway if it is not moved?
options: It is taken to the campus store
It is removed immediately
Its owner is charged a fine
It is moved to the sports hall racks
items.correctAnswer: It is taken to the campus store
items.answerRationale: Stated: tagged, then removed to the campus store if not moved within three days.
distractorRationales: CORRECT
Contradicts the three-day window - the key detail to notice.
No fine is mentioned.
The sports hall is where riders should park voluntarily, not where tagged bicycles go.

items.prompt: When can a tagged bicycle be collected?
options: At any time
Only on weekends
On weekday mornings
Within three days only
items.answerRationale: The facilities desk is open on weekday mornings only.
distractorRationales: Contradicted by "only".
Inverts the stated opening pattern.
CORRECT
Three days is the tagging window, not the collection window - a nearby-number trap.

items.prompt: What is the writer's main point?
options: Students should never reread their notes
Rereading feels effective but recalling from memory works better
Exams mainly reward familiarity with material
Taking good notes matters more than reviewing them
items.correctAnswer: Rereading feels effective but recalling from memory works better
items.answerRationale: The whole passage contrasts the feeling of fluency with the effectiveness of retrieval, and the final paragraph refuses the absolute position.
distractorRationales: Overstates; the last paragraph explicitly rejects this - the strongest distractor.
CORRECT
The passage argues familiarity misleads, not that exams reward it.
Note-taking quality is never compared with reviewing notes.

items.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to learners who keep using retrieval?
options: They read more quickly
They feel less anxious before exams
They need shorter study sessions
They remember more a week later
items.correctAnswer: They remember more a week later
items.answerRationale: Stated directly of those who persist.
distractorRationales: Reading speed is not claimed.
The passage says retrieval feels worse, not calmer.
Session length is never discussed.
CORRECT

items.prompt: In the passage, "the illusion of fluency" refers to
options: the sense that one is reading faster than one really is
the impression that one speaks more smoothly than one actually does
the belief that a short text must be an easy text
the feeling that familiar material has already been learned
items.correctAnswer: the feeling that familiar material has already been learned
items.answerRationale: The meaning comes from the surrounding sentences, not from the term: familiarity is easily mistaken for knowledge, and smooth words on a fourth reading lead the student to conclude the content is secure. All four options are readings the phrase permits on its own, so the passage is required to choose between them.
distractorRationales: A reading-speed interpretation the term allows in isolation; the passage never claims the student misjudges how fast they read.
Transfers the term to spoken fluency; the passage is about reading and recall only.
A text-difficulty interpretation; the passage never mentions length.
CORRECT

items.prompt: In the second paragraph, "it" in "it feels worse" refers to
options: rereading the notes
the exam itself
retrieving information from memory
abandoning studying altogether
items.answerRationale: The pronoun continues the subject of the preceding clause, retrieval, which is described as slower.
distractorRationales: The method being contrasted, and the nearest competing noun phrase.
Not the subject of the sentence.
CORRECT
Appears later in the same sentence as the consequence, not the referent.

items.prompt: In the passage, "that trade-off" means accepting
options: fewer volunteers in return for lower running costs
longer opening hours in return for shorter lines
repairing fewer kinds of item in return for better quality
slower, messier service in return for teaching owners to repair
items.correctAnswer: slower, messier service in return for teaching owners to repair
items.answerRationale: The phrase points back to the explicit comparison: teaching is slower and messier, and lines grow, but the owner gains the skill.
distractorRationales: Costs are never discussed.
Reverses the direction - lines get longer, not shorter.
Range of items is discussed only in the final paragraph, on a different point.
CORRECT

items.prompt: What can be inferred about why owners do the repair work themselves?
options: The volunteers lack the skills to do it for them
So that they can handle similar problems without help later
The cafe cannot accept responsibility for damage
It is quicker than waiting to be served
items.correctAnswer: So that they can handle similar problems without help later
items.answerRationale: Not stated. It follows from the organizers' reason for rejecting a free service: otherwise the owner is no better placed next time.
distractorRationales: Contradicted - volunteers guide the repair.
CORRECT
A realistic institutional motive the passage never raises; the most tempting outside-knowledge answer.
Contradicted - the guided method is slower.

items.prompt: What does the final paragraph suggest about the cafe's list of sealed products?
options: It has become useful beyond the cafe itself
It proves most appliances cannot be repaired
It is used to turn certain customers away
It has replaced the cafe's repair work
items.correctAnswer: It has become useful beyond the cafe itself
items.answerRationale: The list is now shared with a consumer group that uses it in campaigns, so its value has extended outside; this is implied by the handover rather than stated as significance.
distractorRationales: CORRECT
Overgeneralizes from "some appliances" - the main quantifier trap.
Nothing suggests refusing customers.
The repair work continues; the list is a by-product.

tasks.prompt: Talk about a place where you usually study or work. Say where it is, when you normally go there, and why it suits you.
tasks.instructions: You will have 15 seconds to think, then 45 seconds to speak. Speak for as long as you can within the time.
tasks.constructRationale: A familiar, concrete topic every learner in the target population can attempt, so the task elicits speech rather than testing topic knowledge. Three sub-questions give a weaker speaker a structure to follow while leaving a stronger speaker room to elaborate, which is what makes the same prompt informative across the D1-D2 span.

tasks.prompt: Some people prefer to study with other people; others prefer to study alone. Which do you think works better, and why? Give at least one reason and one example from your own experience.
tasks.instructions: You will have 30 seconds to think, then 60 seconds to speak. Try to give reasons, not only your preference.
tasks.constructRationale: Deliberately different evidence from task 1: this one requires taking a position and supporting it, so it can show organisation and connected speech rather than description. The topic needs no specialist knowledge, and both positions are equally defensible so no learner is penalised for their view.

tasks.prompt: You agreed to meet a classmate tomorrow to work on a shared assignment, but you can no longer come. Write a short message to your classmate. In your message: explain why you cannot come, suggest another time, and ask them to send you one thing you need for the assignment.
tasks.instructions: Write 60-90 words. You have about 7 minutes.
tasks.wordGuidanceRationale: Three required functions need roughly 15-25 words each to realise. 60 words is the floor at which all three can appear; above about 90 the task stops producing new evidence and starts consuming time that the second writing task uses better. Derived from the 46-minute design target and this task's grading needs, not from any published exam's limits.

tasks.prompt: Your university is considering making one lecture each week available as a recording instead of teaching it in person. Do you think this is a good idea? Write your opinion and give at least two reasons for it.
tasks.instructions: Write 90-130 words. You have about 9 minutes.
tasks.wordGuidanceRationale: An opinion plus two developed reasons needs roughly 90 words before organisation becomes observable at all. The 130-word ceiling keeps the task inside its 9-minute slot and keeps responses short enough to grade consistently. Chosen for this placement purpose, not copied from an external exam.
targetEvidence: range beyond the prompt's own wording

languageUse.note: Auxiliary diagnostic dimension. overallWeight = 0. These items never substitute for a skill measurement; they exist to sharpen later recommendations.

items.prompt: Quiet, please - I ____ to hear the instructions.
options: try
am trying
tried
have tried
items.answerRationale: An action in progress at the moment of speaking requires the present continuous.
distractorRationales: Present simple; the habitual reading is the common error here.
CORRECT
Past simple, inconsistent with "please" in the same breath.
Present perfect, which implies a completed attempt.
items.diagnosticUse: Weakness here suggests starting with basic tense-aspect contrasts.

items.prompt: The session starts ____ half past nine.
options: on
in
at
to
items.answerRationale: For the exact start time in this sentence, use "at": "The session starts at half past nine." Other prepositions are possible with a clock time in other frames - "by half past nine", "from half past nine" - so the rule is about this slot, not about clock times in general.
distractorRationales: Used with days and dates; it does not mark a named clock time.
Used with months, years and other longer periods.
CORRECT
Belongs to telling the time relative to the next hour, as in "ten to nine"; it cannot fill this slot.
items.diagnosticUse: Weakness here points to prepositions of time as an early vocabulary-grammar target.

items.prompt: We ____ in this building since September.
options: have studied
studied
study
are studying
items.answerRationale: "Since" with a period continuing to now requires the present perfect.
distractorRationales: CORRECT
Past simple, incompatible with "since" plus a continuing period - the central contrast being tested.
Present simple, which cannot carry "since".
Present continuous; tempting because the situation is ongoing, but it does not license "since" here.
items.diagnosticUse: Weakness here suggests work on perfect aspect and time expressions.

items.prompt: Could you ____ me a favor and check the room number?
options: make
do
give
take
items.answerRationale: "Do someone a favor" is the fixed collocation.
distractorRationales: The classic make/do confusion for this noun.
CORRECT
Grammatical but not the established collocation.
Collocates with other nouns, not "favor".
items.diagnosticUse: Weakness here points to collocation work rather than more grammar rules.

items.prompt: Her main ____ to the group project was the data analysis.
options: contribute
contributing
contribution
contributor
items.answerRationale: The slot after a possessive and adjective needs an abstract noun naming the thing contributed.
distractorRationales: Base verb in a noun slot.
Gerund; grammatically possible in other frames but not after "Her main" with this meaning.
CORRECT
A person noun, so it names the wrong referent - the sharpest distractor because it is a real noun.
items.diagnosticUse: Weakness here suggests word-family and suffix work for academic vocabulary.
